blocks.text: A cup of tea at 80 °C is hotter than a bath at 40 °C, yet the bath will scald you far more severely. The tea has the higher temperature but the bath holds vastly more heat. Confusing the two is the single biggest source of lost marks in thermal physics.

blocks.title: Heat and temperature
blocks.text: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a cooler one; it is measured in joules and depends on how much substance there is. Temperature is the degree of hotness of a body, a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules; it is measured in kelvin or degrees Celsius and does not depend on quantity.

blocks.markdown:
### Thermometric properties

A thermometer works by using some physical property that changes measurably and reproducibly with temperature. That property is called a **thermometric property**. A good one must vary continuously, be reversible, and change by a reasonable amount over the range you want to measure.

rows: Pressure of a fixed mass of gas
E.m.f. across a junction of two metals
Rapidly changing or very small regions
Colour and intensity of radiation emitted
Furnaces and molten metal, without contact
blocks.caption: Thermometers and the properties they exploit

blocks.markdown:
### Fixed points and scales

To build a scale you need two reproducible **fixed points**:

- **Lower fixed point (ice point):** the temperature of pure melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure, defined as $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
- **Upper fixed point (steam point):** the temperature of steam above pure boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, defined as $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

The **Kelvin** (absolute) scale uses the same size of degree but starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which molecular motion is at its minimum:

$$T(\text{K}) = \theta(^\circ\text{C}) + 273$$

blocks.title: Calibrating a mercury-in-glass thermometer
blocks.prompt: The mercury thread of an uncalibrated thermometer is 2.0 cm long at the ice point and 22.0 cm long at the steam point. When the bulb is placed in a warm liquid the thread is 12.0 cm long. Calculate the temperature of the liquid.

steps.text: Identify the three readings of the thermometric property, here the thread length.
Evaluate the temperature with its unit.
Note that you must subtract the ice-point reading. Using 12 ÷ 22 × 100 would wrongly give 54.5 °C.

blocks.answer: 50 °C, which is 323 K on the absolute scale

items: Mercury is opaque and shiny, so the thread is easy to see against the scale.
Mercury expands uniformly over a wide range, giving evenly spaced divisions.
Mercury is a good conductor of heat, so the thermometer responds quickly.
Mercury does not wet or stick to glass, so the thread falls back cleanly.
Mercury has a high boiling point (357 °C), which suits high-temperature work.
Alcohol is preferred for very cold conditions because it freezes only at −112 °C.

blocks.title: Why the clinical thermometer has a constriction
blocks.text: A clinical thermometer has a narrow kink just above the bulb. When the thermometer is removed from the patient, the mercury thread breaks at the constriction so the reading is held while you read it. You then shake the thermometer to return the mercury to the bulb.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Gas laws demand absolute temperature. Convert to kelvin by adding 273 the moment you read a Celsius value in a gas question — before any substitution. Forgetting this converts an easy calculation into a guaranteed wrong answer.

points: Heat is energy in transit measured in joules; temperature is degree of hotness measured in kelvin or °C.
A thermometric property is any measurable property that varies reproducibly with temperature.
The ice point (0 °C) and steam point (100 °C) are the two fixed points of the Celsius scale.
Convert Celsius to kelvin by adding 273; absolute zero is −273 °C.
Calibrate using θ = (X_θ − X_0) ÷ (X_100 − X_0) × 100, always subtracting the ice-point value first.
